title: Garry Tan on YC: make something people want, founder mode, and founder psychology
summary: Garry Tan explains how YC runs as a managed network-effects marketplace, why founders should be in the Bay Area, and how self-awareness shapes startups. He also covers co-founder conflict, fundraising as a starting gun, craft in building, and his prompt-iteration workflow with AI.

principles.text: Make something people want: get real paying, retaining customers early, and fundraising becomes easy.
principles.quote: the number one thing that a startup founder can do going into YC is like make really really valuable things and get real customers that you know pay and retain and then fundraising is easy because everyone can see it.

principles.text: Fundraising is the starting gun, not the finish line; treat raised money like debt to return at a big multiple.
principles.quote: I was like, "No, no, no. That's not the finish line. That's the starting gun, guys."

principles.text: Great co-founders fight constantly but preserve the relationship; suppressing disagreement backfires.
principles.quote: Great co-founders fight absolutely all the time and about everything, but mainly because they care so much and they do it in a way that like preserves the relationship.

principles.text: A startup takes on its founder's patterns, so inner work improves hiring, firing and conflict handling.
principles.quote: how you do anything you know how you do anything is how you do everything right

principles.text: Location matters: staying in the Bay Area makes a billion-dollar outcome about 2.5x more likely.
principles.quote: It's two and a half times more likely if people choose to stay in the Bay Area that their company ends up being worth a billion dollars.

principles.text: Evolve your prompts: feed inputs and outputs to an LLM, then ask for the next version of the prompt each iteration.
principles.quote: you'd be like give me the next version of the prompt
